resources.string: Choose how your times are calculated. Nothing is chosen for you, and you can change any of this later.
Each method sets how dawn (Fajr) and night (Isha) are judged. Different communities follow different methods, so times can differ by a few minutes.

If you do not know which method your community follows, ask your local masjid. You can change it here later, and the app will never change it for you. To continue now, you can start with the Muslim World League method and confirm it later.
This sets how the afternoon (Asr) prayer is worked out, and can move Asr later in the day.
Times are calculated for one city. Search the offline list, or use your location to suggest the nearest one.
Optional. Suggests the nearest city from your approximate location, used once and never saved.
Location is off. Search for a city instead.
Couldn\'t get your location. Search for a city instead.
Change your city or how times are calculated. Nothing changes until you save, and the app never changes these for you.
Fajr 18°, Isha 17°. Used widely in Europe and by many communities.
Fajr 18°, Isha 18°. Common in South Asia, including Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Fajr 18.5°, Isha 90 minutes after Maghrib. Used in Saudi Arabia.
Fajr 19.5°, Isha 17.5°. Used in Egypt and parts of Africa.
Fajr 18°, Isha 18°, with a seasonal adjustment at high latitudes. Used by some communities in the UK and North America.
Fajr and Isha 18.2°. Used in the Gulf region.
Fajr 18°, Isha 90 minutes after Maghrib. Used in Qatar.
Fajr 20°, Isha 18°. Used in Singapore and parts of Southeast Asia.
Fajr 15°, Isha 15°. Used by some communities in North America.
Shadow length 2×, which places Asr later in the day.

At high latitudes the sun may not reach the Fajr or Isha angle, so this rule limits how far those times can go. It changes nothing at most latitudes. If you are not sure, the middle of the night is the most permissive limit. The Moonsighting Committee method does not use this rule, and applies its own seasonal adjustment instead.
Fajr is never earlier, and Isha never later, than the middle of the night.
Fajr is no earlier than the last seventh of the night; Isha no later than the end of the first seventh.
The limit is the fraction of the night that this method\'s Fajr and Isha angles imply.
Not used by this method: it applies its own seasonal adjustment at high latitude instead.
Fajr here comes from the high-latitude rule instead of true dawn: on this date at this latitude, true dawn either is not reached or falls beyond this rule\'s limit.
Isha here comes from the high-latitude rule instead of true dusk: on this date at this latitude, true dusk either is not reached or falls beyond this rule\'s limit.
Fajr and Isha here come from the high-latitude rule instead of true dawn and dusk: on this date at this latitude, they either are not reached or fall beyond this rule\'s limit.
Times cannot be calculated for %1$s on this date: at this latitude and time of year the sun neither rises nor sets.
Hijri date: calculated, on the Umm al-Qura convention
Calculated, so it can differ by a day or more from the date your country or community announces. This is not a confirmed local sighting.
Your Hijri date is showing one day earlier.
Your Hijri date is showing one day later.

Counts whatever you name. The app bundles no text of its own and attributes none — the label is your own words, kept on this device.
